content: The International Code of Conduct on Pesticide Management, published in 2014 by the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) and the World Health Organization (WHO), does not express any opinion regarding the legal status of any country, territory, city, or area, nor does it address the delimitation of their frontiers or boundaries. Any dotted lines on maps included in the publication represent approximate borderlines, which may not yet have full agreement. The mention of specific companies or products, whether patented or not, does not imply endorsement or recommendation by FAO or WHO over other similar products not mentioned. Proprietary product names are distinguished by initial capital letters, and all reasonable precautions have been taken by FAO and WHO to verify the information contained in the publication. It must also be clear that FAO and WHO do not endorse the users’ views, products, or services in any way. The International Code of Conduct on Pesticide Management, now in its fourth version since its initial approval in 1985, provides a comprehensive framework for guiding governments, the private sector, civil society, and other stakeholders on best practices in managing pesticides throughout their lifecycle. This version, approved in 2013, incorporates public health pesticides and vector control, broadening its scope beyond agricultural pesticides. It emphasizes health and environmental aspects, updates definitions and terms, and aligns technical guidance with developments in international chemical management. The Code comes at a time when there is increased focus on enhancing food production while conserving and improving the natural resources that support it. Healthy ecosystems are more productive, resilient to shocks, and capable of maintaining pests and diseases at acceptable levels. The FAO’s strategic framework has been reoriented to support sustainable agricultural production, with the Code serving as an integral component of this objective. Integrated Pest Management (IPM), which has successfully reduced pesticide use and improved yields, food quality, and farmer incomes, is a key approach promoted by the Code. The Code also highlights the importance of providing farmers with access to locally adapted, high-quality seeds and planting materials to prevent the spread of pests and diseases. Protecting soils and ensuring adequate nutrient and water availability for crops result in healthier plants that are more resistant to pest and disease attacks. Holistic approaches, such as those outlined in the FAO publication Save and Grow, help reduce reliance on pesticides and other external inputs, yielding economic, health, and environmental benefits for farmers and consumers. The International Code of Conduct on Pesticide Management is a voluntary framework endorsed by FAO members and supported by key pesticide industry associations and civil society organizations. It complements legally binding instruments such as the Rotterdam Convention, the Stockholm Convention, and the Basel Convention, as well as voluntary mechanisms like the Strategic Approach to International Chemicals Management (SAICM). Pesticides, as an important group of chemicals, require careful management to maximize their benefits while minimizing risks to health and the environment. The Code provides voluntary standards of conduct for all entities involved in or associated with pesticide management, particularly in contexts where national legislation is inadequate or absent. It addresses governments, international organizations, the pesticide industry, application equipment manufacturers, pesticide traders, pest control operators, the food industry, pesticide users, and public-interest groups such as environmental and consumer organizations. It emphasizes the shared responsibility of these sectors to ensure that the necessary and acceptable use of pesticides achieves its benefits without significant adverse effects on human and animal health or the environment. The Code also recognizes the need for cooperative efforts between pesticide-exporting and importing countries to promote practices that minimize health and environmental risks while ensuring effective pesticide use. It highlights the importance of training and capacity-building at all levels to implement and observe its provisions effectively. Entities addressed by the Code are encouraged to prioritize relevant training and capacity-building activities. The Code promotes participation in information exchange and international agreements, such as the Rotterdam Convention on the Prior Informed Consent (PIC) Procedure for Certain Hazardous Chemicals and Pesticides in International Trade. It also provides definitions for key terms, such as active ingredient, advertising, application equipment, application technology, banned pesticide, co-formulant, container, disposal, distribution, environment, equivalence, extension service, formulation, and Good Agricultural Practice (GAP). These definitions ensure clarity and consistency in the implementation of the Code’s provisions. The Code emphasizes the importance of identifying and, if necessary, removing highly hazardous pesticides from use to protect vulnerable groups such as children, women, and individuals affected by HIV/AIDS. It strongly recommends minimizing pesticide use and adopting integrated vector management for controlling vector-borne diseases. By strengthening the capacity of developing countries to regulate, evaluate, and enforce effective control over pesticides, the Code aims to reduce health and environmental risks while improving productivity, sustainability, and livelihoods for farmers worldwide.
